LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson stretches: your child hisses a sound that can outlast anyone’s patience, points to the teeth doing the work, becomes a sunbeam on command and traces the curviest letter yet.

What is this?

S is the nineteenth letter of the alphabet. Big S and little s make the s sound — sss, a hiss like a snake or a tyre letting air out gently. The teeth do the work; the breath does the rest.

What does it mean?

S is the stretchiest sound in the set: long, short, loud or whispery, one letter with an entire orchestra of practice. And sun is a word children meet in books long before breakfast.

What does the child need to know?

The letter is called S; the sound is sss — a clean hiss, voice off, teeth nearly together. Stretch it long or clip it short; either way the throat stays quiet, because a buzzing sss is Z sneaking in.

Why this matters

A sound with a built-in contest (who runs out of air first?) and a built-in game (freeze as a sunbeam) fills a whole afternoon. The smiling sun on the card does half the welcoming by itself.

What it teaches

Long-airflow hiss control, teeth placement awareness, voice-off discrimination, letter recognition in two cases, and whole-body stillness on cue — freeze games train the stopping muscle as much as the starting one.

Words to learn

Ssunssshissstretchfreeze

Say this to your child

“"This is the letter S — hello, S! S says sss — a hiss, like a snake in the grass. Teeth together, breath out: sssss. How long can you hold it? Now be a sunbeam — arms out, turn around slowly... sss-sun! Freeze! Lovely and sunny. Then trace the big S: slide down like a snake."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and squint at it: this is the letter S, and this is the sun — smiling, with rays to point at.
  2. Make the hiss: teeth nearly closed, breath sliding out — sssss. Point at your own teeth: they are the players. Try a long sss, then three short ones.
  3. Trace big S — one winding curve from top to bottom, like a snake sliding downhill — and little s: the same wiggle, smaller.
  4. Play sunbeams: stretch your arms out wide, turn slowly while hissing sss-sun, and freeze into a sunny statue the moment you call freeze.
  5. End with an s-hunt: find three things that start with the hiss — a sock, a spoon, a smile — and hiss the sound at each one.

Look closer at the picture

Find the big uppercase S and the little lowercase s on the card, then the smiling sun and the word Sun. Ask which letter wiggles more — both Ss wind down the page in curves, one big and one small.

Ask your child

"What is this letter called?" "What sound does S make?" "Can your hiss beat mine for length?" "Can you freeze like a sunbeam?" — answered with a name, a clean sss, an epic breath-off and one statue-still sunbeam.

What your child can say or do

"Sss! Sss-sun!" Expect hisses at snakes in books, s-sounds offered to socks and sausages, and sunbeam freezing whenever music stops anywhere in the house. The hiss contest may settle sibling disputes. Possibly not peacefully.

Out in the real world

S hisses through the day: sun on the curtains, soup at lunch, sleep at bedtime, the slide at the park. Every hiss is the card rehearsing — and every sunny morning is the letter arriving in the window.

Try it together

Sss contest: faces close, one long hiss each — first out of air becomes the sun for the next round, arms out wide while everyone hisses at them. Then the sun hisses back. Nobody truly wins; everybody practises.

Understanding check

Ask what S says: a long clean hiss with voice off means the sound landed — check the throat stays quiet, because buzzing means z sneaked in. A wiggly little s traced in the air completes the sunshine.

Parent tips

S invites exaggeration — let the hisses be enormous at first, then normal-sized. If a buzz appears, that is Z’s sound visiting; keep your own throat silent and let your child find the quiet version by listening.

Staying safe

Sunbeam spinning happens in cleared space, slow turns only, with breaks before dizziness wins. Real sunshine needs hats and shade; the hissing can move indoors, where the freezing is safer anyway.

This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).
